dok_rationale: Part (c) coordinates the formal evidence decision, practical importance, and study design to repair two competing conclusions and state a justified population claim.
stem: A cafeteria served 5{,}000 September trays after new sorting-bin labels were installed. The director claims at least $60\%$ are sorted correctly. An SRS of 250 trays finds 136 correct; the club tests at $\alpha=0.05$.\par\smallskip \textbf{Imani:} ``The $p$-value is 0.0354, so reject $H_0$. The labels caused sorting below 60 percent for every month.''\par \textbf{Drew:} ``The 5.6-point gap may be too small to matter, so it is not significant. Accept the director's claim.''\par\smallskip The test conditions have been checked: random sample; $250<500$; null-expected counts 150 and 100.
first_take: Can these September trays tell us what caused the result in every month? Give one reason from the study.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define $p$ and state the hypotheses for checking whether correct sorting is below 60\%.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate $\widehat p$, the one-proportion $z$ statistic, and the lower-tail $p$-value. Use the verified conditions above.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: In 4--5 sentences, correct both reports. Compare the $p$-value with $\alpha$, separate statistical significance from practical importance, and limit the conclusion to the people or items studied and what the design can show about cause.

answers.a: Let $p$ be the proportion of all 5,000 September trays sorted correctly. Test $H_0:p=0.60$ versus $H_a:p<0.60$.
answers.b: $\widehat p=136/250=0.544$. Random is supported by the stated SRS. The 10 percent condition holds because $250<0.10(5{,}000)=500$. Under $H_0$, $np_0=250(0.60)=150$ and $n(1-p_0)=250(0.40)=100$, both at least 10. Thus $SE_0=\sqrt{0.60(0.40)/250}=0.0309839$ and $z=(0.544-0.60)/0.0309839=-1.8074$. The lower-tail normal probability is $P(Z\leq-1.8074)=0.0354$.
answers.c: Imani correctly rejects $H_0$ because $0.0354<0.05$: there is convincing evidence that fewer than 60\% of September trays were sorted correctly. Drew can question whether the 5.6-percentage-point sample gap matters in practice, but that does not reverse the statistical decision or establish the null claim. The SRS represents September trays. Without random assignment and a comparison group, the study does not show that the labels caused the result. It also cannot establish what happens every month.

expectedElements.description: Uses 0.0354<0.05 to reject and concludes below 60 percent for September trays.
Explains that practical importance cannot reverse the significance decision or establish the null.
Limits inference to September and withholds label causation because there was no randomized comparison.

scoringGuide.E: Meets all three checks with correct contextual reasoning; equivalent wording is acceptable.
scoringGuide.P: Shows at least one substantive correct check, but has an omission or error that prevents E.
scoringGuide.I: Shows none of the three checks with substantive correct reasoning; a choice alone is insufficient.
